name: keras
title: Keras: The Multi-Backend Deep Learning API for AI Development
answer: Keras is an open-source Python deep learning API, maintained by the Keras team and released under Apache-2.0, that lets you build and train neural networks with a high-level, readable interface. Since Keras 3 it runs on JAX, TensorFlow, PyTorch, or OpenVINO, so the same model code can move between backends. If you are deciding whether to use it, the key point is that it favors fast, standard workflows over low-level control, and its official site is a full learning resource.

sections.body: Keras is a deep learning framework for Python, described on its official site as deep learning for humans, and distributed under the Apache-2.0 licence from the keras-team/keras repository. It sits at the model-building layer of the AI stack, offering high-level abstractions for layers, models, losses, optimizers, metrics, and training loops rather than the tensor-level primitives underneath. The site's Keras 3 page marks a major shift: Keras workflows can now run on top of JAX, TensorFlow, PyTorch, or OpenVINO for inference only, and Keras can act as a low-level cross-framework language for custom layers, models, or metrics usable in native JAX, TensorFlow, or PyTorch workflows from one codebase. The repository shows active development, with a last push in October 2026 and more than 64,000 stars.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: The official guides show Keras used for the core jobs of applied deep learning: defining models, training with fit(), evaluating with evaluate(), and predicting, all with the same routines across Sequential models, models built with the functional API, and models written by subclassing. The functional API covers non-linear topology, shared layers, and multiple inputs or outputs, and the site's examples extend to autoencoders, transfer learning for image classification, sample-size estimation, and a mini-GPT text generation model built with KerasHub. Keras 3 adds a distribution API for model parallelism, data parallelism, and combinations of both, currently implemented for the JAX backend. It is strongest when you want standard, well-documented workflows and the freedom to switch backends, and the site reports that JAX typically delivers the best training and inference performance on GPU, TPU, and CPU in benchmarks, though results vary by model.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: Keras is designed to be approachable. The Sequential guide starts from a plain stack of layers and explains that layers need to know their input shape before they can create weights, and that a model without an input shape is not built and has no weights. The functional API guide assumes you can specify input shapes such as (32, 32, 3) and omit batch size. The built-in training guide expects familiarity with loss functions, optimizers, and metrics, and shows how to configure them through compile(). The official site offers guides, examples, and API references that a beginner can follow, but it does not present Keras as a substitute for understanding the mathematics of neural networks or the systems underneath, and the material read does not state formal prerequisites.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: The official site documents a broad ecosystem. Keras 3 implements the full Keras API across TensorFlow, JAX, and PyTorch, including over a hundred layers, dozens of metrics, loss functions, optimizers, callbacks, training and evaluation loops, and saving and serialization infrastructure. The keras.ops namespace works across all backends and includes ops.matmul, ops.sum, ops.stack, ops.einsum, and neural network functions such as ops.softmax, ops.binary_crossentropy, and ops.conv. KerasHub supports pretrained models and layers, as shown in the mini-GPT example. The site reports that Keras has been chosen by over 2.5 million developers and powers systems such as the Waymo self-driving fleet and the YouTube recommendation engine. The repository's star count and recent activity indicate a large, active community, though the pages read do not quantify forum or support channels.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: Keras is built for both quick experiments and production use, with trade-offs. The Sequential and functional APIs let you define and train a model in a few lines, and the built-in fit(), evaluate(), and predict() loops handle batching, validation splits, and metrics without custom code. For production, Keras 3 offers backend choice, so you can move a model to JAX for performance or keep it in TensorFlow, and the distribution API supports model and data parallelism, currently on JAX. Saving the entire model as a single file preserves the optimizer state so training can resume. The cost is that the highest-level abstractions hide some low-level control, and the site notes that benchmark results vary from model to model, so backend choice still needs measurement.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: The official site states that Keras has been chosen by over 2.5 million developers and powers systems such as the Waymo self-driving fleet and the YouTube recommendation engine. That places it among the current standards for applied deep learning rather than a legacy choice, and the Keras 3 release keeps it aligned with JAX, TensorFlow, and PyTorch. For someone choosing what to learn for work, the site's emphasis on one codebase across backends and on existing tf.keras models running in JAX and PyTorch suggests transferable skills. The pages read do not provide job-market statistics, salary data, or employer surveys, so claims about hiring demand cannot be grounded in this material.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: Keras is a Python library that sits above backend engines rather than replacing them. The Keras 3 page describes it as a cross-framework language: a Keras model can be instantiated as a PyTorch Module, exported as a TensorFlow SavedModel, or instantiated as a stateless JAX function. Training routines accept tf.data.Dataset objects, PyTorch DataLoader objects, NumPy arrays, and Pandas dataframes regardless of backend. Custom layers written only with keras.ops work across JAX, PyTorch, and TensorFlow with the same code. This is the polyglot pattern the site presents: one high-level API, several execution engines, and interoperability with the surrounding Python data and model ecosystem.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: The official material is clear about some boundaries. The Sequential model is not appropriate for non-linear topology such as residual connections or multi-branch models, where the functional API is needed. The distribution API is currently implemented for the JAX backend, with TensorFlow and PyTorch support described as coming soon, so parallelism features are not yet uniform. Benchmark performance varies by model, and the site does not promise that JAX is always fastest. The pages read do not cover deployment tooling, mobile or edge runtimes beyond OpenVINO inference, security, or long-term support timelines, and they do not state formal prerequisites or quantify community support channels, so those questions remain open.
sections.heading: Limits and open questions
